To address this, researchers have developed various dynamic graph modeling techniques to capture temporal changes. We present a framework that combines multi-modal perception with actuation using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to ensure smooth control outputs. First, the model is trained to perform a specific task using a deep encoder to extract state embeddings and a deep decoder that generates a distribution over possible decoder actions. Subsequently, the trained model is fine-tuned through an unsupervised self-supervision process to predict both the actuator forces required for movement and the subsequent actuator outcomes. This fine-tuning employs a variational autoencoder (VAE) trained on pairs of predicted actuator inputs and outputs, with the VAE's latent space representing the probability density function of the actuator inputs, which is then used to model the environment's reward function for training. We evaluated this approach on two continuous robotics tasks—navigating a mobile robot to grasp an object and manipulating a pendulum to reach a target angle—using real-world data. In both experiments, we compared our method against state-of-the-art DRL techniques for task-specific components, such as motion encoding and policy optimization, by benchmarking performance against a baseline policy execution without specific task adaptation, ultimately demonstrating the efficacy of our contribution in achieving successful task completion.

This study introduces an analytical framework for assessing the relative strength of two architectures by employing a novel metric known as "dilation." Unlike the widely known "width," which tracks the volume of data traversing a network, "dilation" captures the minimum number of internal network layers a signal passes through at any point. Ultimately, the proposed simplified metric offers a robust method for evaluating and comparing DNN expressive capabilities.

Results from a thorough analysis and implementation—optimized for modern CPUs and integrated into open-source compilers like LLVM and GCC—reveal that, compared to standard multi-core configurations, our solution can accelerate execution by up to 1.6× while reducing overall energy usage by as much as 2.6×.

First, we present a two-stage Bayesian dynamic programming method for one-to-one matching one-on-one comparisons between pairs of records, determining whether they are matches, nonmatches, or duplicate instances of a common source. In diverse applications, match probability is estimated using the unique attributes of each record, while non-match likelihood is modeled against historical records. This two-step procedure effectively mitigates the combinatorial explosion inherent in conventional two-stage linkage processes by decomposing an exponentially complex many-to-one task into more manageable linear components. This study proposes the Multivariate Blipped Diff-in-Diff (MBlipped) approach to evaluate individual or simultaneous interventions on several outcomes while producing valid estimates. Finally, through both simulated data and an empirical analysis of an agricultural study, we confirm MBlipped's superior performance compared to leading alternative approaches.
